https://www.armstrongeconomics.com/uncat.text: Neocon & Their Lies QUESTION: Do you mind if I ask something personal? It’s clear the neoconservatives aren’t fond of you, and I imagine the feeling is mutual. Since I know you’ve met quite a few of them face-to-face, was there a particular moment or encounter that personally struck a nerve with you? EJ ANSWER: That is an interesting question. Aside from being misled that I initially believed they were economic conservatives, I came to see their disregard for human life and history. I lost high school friends in Vietnam. Others in Iraq. My family has fought in every American war. My cousin still has the musket from the Armstrong who fought in the American Revolution. There’s a profound difference between defending your homeland and being sent to war on false pretenses to satisfy some deranged political theory of world domination. The Vietnam veterans I’ve known are among the most anguished. They carry the weight of knowing, even today, that they were sent to fight for a lie. Neoconservatism, at its core, tends to elevate ideological and strategic goals above the human toll of warfare. That’s certainly a point of fierce political disagreement, but if you look at the ideology, its history, and how it’s played out, it becomes clearer why so many see it that way—and why that perspective feels deeply personal to those of us who’ve lost people along the way. From Project Northwoods willing to kill American civilians just to blame it on Cuba to justify a war to assassinatinge JFK because he sought peace with the USSR. This ideology’s roots goes back to the debunked political theory of Trotskyite ideology of the early 20th Century. This is a reference to the fact that many early neoconservatives were former LEFTISTS who became disillusioned with liberalism and the counterculture of the 1960s . Irving Kristol was a disillusioned liberal who became a foundational figure of neoconservatism. While he held a deep concern for the survival of Israel and wrote about it in those terms, there has always been a debate if he and other were covertly just wanted war to protect Israel in the direct sense. Irving Kristol remained sympathetic to the goals of the New Deal and the Great Society, but he grew skeptical of government planning and what he saw as the vague idealism of left-wing ideologues. He rejected the conservative anti-New Deal stance of Barry Goldwater in 1964, but also distrusted the radical dissent of the counterculture. While he is credited with this dogmatic view, I knew his son and even helped him start his magazine the Weekly Standard taking the back page to kick off his venture. I came to understand that I was wrong. Bill was not about economic conservatism. This was all about geopolitical war and indeed to support Israel. I had discussions about how taking down Saddam Husein in Iraq and then others was necessary to bring peace to the Middle East. This dogmatic view concerned me. Bill Kristol was so anti-Trump because he was against war that he killed his own magazine with his Neocon views. Bill Kristol, the prominent neoconservative commentator and founder of The Weekly Standard, did endorse Kamala Harris for president in the 2024 election along with Dick Cheney. This proved their movement was never about economics. The Neocon ideology is characterized by a strong endorsement of military instruments to promote what is viewed as the U.S. national interest, a concept scholars describe as a mix of “assertive nationalism” and “militarism.” The belief is that American military might should be used to spread democracy and freedom, even by force and without international cooperation if necessary. I disagreed since I believed that the very usurpation of power to effectively create a coup of American foreign policy was taking place before my eyes during Bush Jr’s administration. This was all justified by a powerful sense of American exceptionalism and a moralistic view of the world, dividing it into allies and adversaries I came to see was a reaction to Khrushchev’s (1953-1964) “ we will bury you ” boast of November 18th, 1956 spoken at the Polish Embassy. That boast was standard Communist view that recessions and depression was a flaw of Capitalism and this Marxism would eliminate that. The Neocon stated goal became more radical after Irving to justify using U.S. power to create a world of democracies, which, in their view, are inherently more peaceful. Being a student of political systems, we ourselves did not live under a democracy. I saw a usurpation of power through UNELECTED means to achieve a fake goal of morality that allowed them to look at themselves in the mirror as righteous rather than usurpers seeking to create peace by killing all your enemies. What I write about is not conspiracy theory. For whatever reason, I seem to have ended up in the middle of so many things, which is why they are so determined to try to prevent people from listening to me. https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text: The Palm house at Kew Gardens. The team have already begun emptying out the beds around the site. Photograph: Sarah Lee/The Guardian View image in fullscreen The Palm house at Kew Gardens. The team have already begun emptying out the beds around the site. Photograph: Sarah Lee/The Guardian Kew Gardens ‘Sad moments ahead’: Kew Gardens to fell rare trees in race to save Victorian greenhouse Horticulturalists begin moving and propagating plants before the rusty and warped Palm House begins renovation – but some are too tall to save Helena Horton and George Francis Lee Thu 27 Aug 2026 01.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google It will be a gut-wrenching moment for the horticulturalists at Kew Gardens when some of the magnificent trees in the Palm House have to be felled. “There are some sad moments ahead,” said Palm House manager, Will Spoelstra, who knows all the plants inside the cathedral-like greenhouse. But moving some of the 1,000 plants – and sacrificing others – is crucial as the botanists and horticulturalists at the world’s biggest plant collection, based in south-west London , race against time to renovate the Victorian-era glasshouse. View image in fullscreen Tom Pickering, the head of glasshouses at Kew, looking at a flowering Ramosmania rodriguesii, says the chance to propagate so many of the plants has exciting implications for conservation. Photograph: Sarah Lee/The Guardian The ornate ironwork is rusted and the 16,000 panes of glass it is comprised of are warped and damaged, making it difficult to maintain the hot, humid conditions its rare plants need. Some plants grown within are critically endangered, and in some cases, Kew holds the only specimens. “It is an exciting project,” Spoelstra says, “but we are going to lose some really nice specimens.” The giant palm trees whose fronds grow right to the roof of the building are not exactly portable, so will have to be felled. Kew Gardens’ tropical Palm House to shut for five years for net zero makeover Read more His team have already begun emptying out the beds around the Palm House, which will remain open throughout the renovation project, scheduled to start in 2027 subject to funds being raised in time. “It’s a shame to see the empty beds. Sometimes, I go to where one of my favourite plants was and realise it’s gone!,” Spoelstra says. The plants have been moved to a behind-the-scenes greenhouse, the tropical nursery, where they can get used to the conditions there before moving back into a renovated greenhouse. “Most plants will sulk for a bit when they’re moved,” he said. Kew’s scientists are working to collect seeds and cuttings to propagate new plants to fill the greenhouse. The tropical nursery currently looks like the Palm House in miniature, filled with saplings of the majestic trees they descend from. View image in fullscreen The giant palm trees whose fronds grow right to the roof of the building are not exactly portable, so will have to be felled. Photograph: Sarah Lee/The Guardian The project has also given Kew’s workers an opportunity to do some groundbreaking conservation work. One of the trees that cannot be moved and needs to be cut down due to its size is the Ravenea Moorei , native to the Comoros islands near Madagascar. Scientists were concerned as it was thought to be the only one of its kind. Kew’s specimen is male and cannot produce seed without a female. The researchers went on an expedition to the Comoros in the hope of finding a wild population – and succeeded. Due to its success, the specimen in the greenhouse could be propagated, and there are now 10 young plants in the tropical nursery. Kew will also be helping the scientists in the Comoros protect and enhance the wild population. Some plants will be very perilous to move. The Aiphanes eggersii is covered in large spikes. Spoelstra says: “We are concerned about cutting ourselves on those spikes when we move it, we will have to wrap it well.” But staff at Kew are also excited that they have sown seeds from it for the first time successfully. Kew has enlisted specialist movers who work with rare and fragile works of art to help relocate specimens including the Eastern Cape giant cycad, which is the oldest pot plant in the world and has been growing at Kew since 1775. Though it is propped up by supports, it is still going strong and sprouting new shoots. The chance to propagate so many of the plants has exciting implications for conservation. Tom Pickering, the head of glasshouses at Kew, said: “We can play a major part in conserving plants in the wild. We are thrilled by that, and we think translocation to the wild of our plants will play an even bigger role in the future.” View image in fullscreen Kew’s scientists are working to collect seeds and cuttings to propagate new plants to fill the greenhouse. Photograph: Sarah Lee/The Guardian These plants include the constantly flowering Ramosmania rodriguesii , which Kew successfully cultivated from cuttings taken from its single surviving tree in Rodrigues, Mauritius. Pickering proudly points out young specimens in the tropical nursery which have been successfully propagated. Trees grown at Kew have now been translocated back into the wild. “That was amazingly satisfying,” he says. “We can’t just be a repository of exotic plants, I hope that this can work as a blueprint in horticulture, bringing plants back, and working with partners all over the world.” Kew will be starting a fundraising drive this October to “save London’s rainforest”, but if it all goes to plan the renovation will last for about 50 years. This means the seeds and young plants Pickering is tending in the nursery will be in the Palm House for decades. “It’s nice to think that these plants will be thriving for decades to come, maybe when I am not here any more,” he said. The project has already helped save some plants from extinction in the wild. Pickering said: “Thinking that these plants can become abundant again, there is such a big feeling of hope.” Explore more on these topics Kew Gardens Trees and forests Plants London Rewilding news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: Tents sheltering displaced Palestinians amid the ruins of Gaza City. Maryam and her family were sleeping in tents while she had cancer without any medical facilities to treat her. Photograph: Jehad Alshrafi/AP View image in fullscreen Tents sheltering displaced Palestinians amid the ruins of Gaza City. Maryam and her family were sleeping in tents while she had cancer without any medical facilities to treat her. Photograph: Jehad Alshrafi/AP Immigration and asylum Gaza refugee says sister-in-law ‘would be alive’ if Home Office had let her come to UK Anwar, who lives in Glasgow, says Home Office refused visa application despite Maryam having cancer Diane Taylor Sat 5 Sep 2026 06.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 06.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A man living in the UK has said he believes his sister-in-law who died from cancer in Gaza would still be alive today if the Home Office had agreed to bring her and her family to Britain. Anwar, who lives in Glasgow, fled Gaza in 2020 and was granted refugee status in the UK in 2021. After the destruction of large areas of Gaza by Israeli forces following the Hamas attacks on Israel in October 2023, he applied to bring his brother Hassan, Hassan’s wife, Maryam , their two young children and other family members to the UK in October 2025. He said the Home Office rejected their application. The process required them to travel to a visa application centre (VAC) for biometric checks, but there was not, and still is not, a VAC in Gaza . It is difficult for Palestinians to leave the territory to access a VAC elsewhere. In April this year the family asked the Home Office to waive this requirement and grant permission for “predetermination” of their application and “biometric excusal”. The Home Office is understood to have rejected this request, so the family launched a legal challenge. The Home Office agreed to reconsider its decision but issued a new refusal in July. Prior to the second Home Office refusal, and shortly after Maryam gave birth to Ismail, who is now seven months old, she was diagnosed with renal cell carcinoma, which had spread to her lungs. Doctors in Gaza said they did not have the facilities to treat her. The family provided the Home Office with medical evidence concerning Maryam’s condition, including cancer test results and medical referral reports. They also provided evidence of their living conditions in Gaza, which involved sleeping in tents and shortages of food, medicine and clean water. Anwar said the Home Office again refused the family’s request for predetermination and biometric excusal but that it accepted the evidence of Maryam’s cancer. In the Home Office’s letter refusing the visa application on 31 July, seen by the Guardian, officials stated: “Given the current situation in Gaza, reliable healthcare may not be accessible.” They accepted that Maryam was facing a significant risk of harm because she was in a conflict zone and could not travel to a VAC. Although the Home Office officials found the circumstances relating to travel to a VAC “somewhat compelling”, they concluded that owing to the difficulty in travelling to the VAC, it was “in the best interests of the children to stay with their parents and delay travel to the UK” for the time being. They concluded the family’s situation did not meet the threshold for “compelling circumstances” and said that pre-entry checks needed to be carried out because the family came from “a territory where terrorists operate”. In the legal challenge, the family’s lawyers stated: “It is difficult to understand what circumstances would ever qualify as compelling if the present circumstances do not.” Maryam died from cancer on 28 August. Gordon McKee, the Labour MP for Glasgow South, raised the family’s case with ministers in June. He warned about Maryam’s deteriorating health and the consequences of the collapse of reliable healthcare in Gaza. In his letter to Mike Tapp, then a Home Office minister, McKee said the case involved “exceptional humanitarian circumstances”. He asked Tapp to consider reviewing the case personally. Anwar said: “We believe Maryam’s case raises serious questions about how the UK government deals with Palestinian families in Gaza who are trying to reunite with their families in Britain, particularly when a family member becomes seriously ill while trapped in a conflict zone and unable to safely reach a VAC. “I believe that if the Home Office had agreed to bring Maryam and her family from Gaza to the UK when we first applied last October, Maryam would still be alive today. “Maryam is now gone, but her family remains in Gaza. We are now urgently asking the UK government to intervene to protect Maryam’s surviving family members and to find a way to bring them to safety and reunite them with their family in the UK.” Speaking from Gaza, Maryam’s husband, Hassan, said: “I am struggling to come to terms with losing my wife while I remain trapped in Gaza with our children, including our seven-month-old baby. “Throughout Maryam’s illness, we were trying to find a way for our family to overcome the biometric requirement and move forward with our applications. The Home Office accepted that Maryam had cancer and acknowledged the evidence, but decided that our circumstances were still not compelling enough to justify biometric deferral or predetermination. “Now I have lost my wife, and I am left trying to protect our children and find a way to get them out of Gaza and to safety.” Home Office sources said they did not routinely comment on individual cases. https://www.politico.eu/article/in-ceuta.text: Alberto Núñez Feijóo is Spain’s leader of the opposition and the president of the People’s Party. On July 30, at least 80,000 people crossed into Ceuta from Morocco, the largest violation of territorial integrity we have experienced in recent decades. That challenge tested the resilience of Spain’s southern border and, therefore, of Europe’s southern border. It continues 50 days later. With no clear prospect of when it might be resolved. It is therefore time to ask ourselves whether our response matches the scale of what is at stake. A border is not just a line on a map. It is the expression of a political community that decides which values to protect and which responsibilities to share. When a European border is breached, Europe as a whole becomes weaker. When a border is not properly defended, Europe as a whole is left unprotected. That is what is happening. Advertisement Advertisement The response of the current Spanish government, incapable of acknowledging the true nature of the problem and implementing the correct solution, obliges me to reiterate, first and foremost, the obvious, as the President of Ceuta did last week during his visit to Brussels. We are not witnessing a conventional migration crisis, but rather the consequences of an invasion originating from Morocco, which must therefore be held responsible for having condoned or instigated it. Normality has disappeared from Ceuta for more than six weeks, and the scenes of chaos, overcrowding and insecurity should both shame us and compel us to act. To think that the prolongation of this situation will have no consequences is a mistake we cannot afford to make: it affects our sovereignty, our collective capacity to defend the rule of law, the safety of our citizens, and the credibility of the European project in ensuring its own stability. Undoubtedly, the national authorities are the first to bear the responsibility for resolving this crisis, in accordance with a non-negotiable principle shared by all EU member states under the Pact on Migration and Asylum: those who have entered irregularly must be returned. All of them. The Spanish government’s obligation is not to find accommodation for them, but to expedite their departure. That said, given the time that has elapsed and the escalation of violent incidents in Ceuta, Europe as a whole must recognize the failure of the Spanish government and exert the necessary pressure to prevent this crisis from becoming entrenched, spreading, or happening again. Just as Europe has responded when faced with other hybrid threats — on energy, trade or disinformation — the attack on our southern border now demands the same determination. Firstly, the European Union must ensure that Spain implements, with due rigor and efficiency, all the European instruments available to facilitate returns. Secondly, it must clarify why the Kingdom of Morocco itself has reiterated in an official statement its willingness to take back all those who entered on July 30, while Spanish ministers maintain that no such cooperation exists. Thirdly, it must make full use of all its diplomatic resources to ensure that the relationship with Morocco, a strategic partner for Spain and for the rest of Europe, continues to develop on the basis of transparency and mutual respect. While I advocate the need to establish a loyal and stable relationship with our neighboring country, I believe it is in the interests of the entire European Union to ensure that this relationship is not undermined by the exploitation of migration flows or by the questioning of the Spanish identity of Ceuta and Melilla, territories that are just as European as Berlin, Paris or Brussels. Advertisement Advertisement Finally, I would like to stress that humanity cannot be used as an excuse for inaction in response to what has happened. It is true that the attack on Ceuta did not involve soldiers, that many of those who crossed Europe’s southern border were themselves victims and that, in fact, more than a hundred people died. But contrary to what some cynically claim, it is precisely humanity that compels us to discourage people from risking their lives at sea: this must cease to be a valid means of reaching Europe. As many know, I aspire to become the next prime minister of Spain. Consequently, it is my duty to seek the support of the European Union and all of its member states for my country at this crucial moment. The first duty of a leader is to guarantee the safety of citizens, defend national sovereignty and uphold the credibility of institutions. But this also reflects a commitment to a certain way of understanding Europe, one that I personally share with all our allies: the responsibility to safeguard its territorial integrity and its values is a shared one. Now it is our turn to defend Ceuta, Spain and Europe. The views expressed are those of the authors and do not reflect the views of POLITICO.

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/tur.text: VLCC Tanker Market Firming Once More Clean tanker markets size up impact of potential US diesel export curbs Dry Bulk Shipping: China Soybean Imports on the Rise Widening Gap On Green Goals Baltic Dry Bulk Freight Index Edges Up On Capesize Gains Turkey seeks Black Sea shipping deal as attacks threaten grain trade in International Shipping News 21/09/2026 Turkey is racing to restore safe passage for cargo ships in the Black Sea as attacks on shipping disrupt grain exports and push up prices. Russia and Ukraine are major global wheat exporters, but Black Sea trade has been severely disrupted as both sides step up attacks on shipping and port infrastructure. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan announced this week that Turkey was working on a plan to ensure safe passage in the Black Sea for commercial shipping and said he was in touch with both Ukraine and Russia. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan confirmed that he raised the issue with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, on the sidelines of a gathering of regional leaders in Kyrgyzstan. The Turkish move comes as Ukraine and Russia have ramped up their attacks on shipping and ports in and around the Black Sea. In 2022, Turkey and the United Nations brokered a deal between Ukraine and Russia to ensure safe passage for Ukrainian grain exports through the Black Sea. The agreement lasted a year. While Turkey has maintained good ties with both sides, reaching another agreement will be much harder, warned international relations professor Huseyin Bagci of Ankara’s Middle East Technical University. “The tension is increasing more than ever before,” Bagci said. “It’s not enough to have good relations, because the two sides – the Ukrainians and Russians – should sit down and talk about a common solution to this problem. Turkey cannot solve this problem alone.” Growing attacks In August Ukraine offered a ceasefire on commercial shipping, but the offer was rejected by Moscow, which said it wanted a broader deal. Ukrainian drones continue to strike Russian shipping, while Russia has continued missile attacks on Ukrainian ports and ships. This surge in attacks comes as both nations rush to export their grain harvests. Grain prices have risen sharply, by as much as 30 percent, international grain broker Can Atbasoglu said, even as both sides scramble to find new routes for their exports. “Russia will do their best to export as much as they can, both from Russian Baltic ports and EU Baltic ports like Latvia and Lithuania; they’re also exporting,” Atbasoglu said. “Ukraine will also export as much as they can from Romania as well and through the Danube ports. But the export pace will be definitely lower. So it will definitely stay bullish for the markets. Prices are definitely going to stay like this or can have a further increase.” Ships staying put At one of Istanbul’s many shipyards, the docks are crowded with ships that once braved the Black Sea. One vessel bears the scars of a drone attack and is under repair. Others undergo routine maintenance as shipowners hesitate to risk new journeys into dangerous waters. The superintendent of one ship, speaking anonymously, says repairs are nearly finished, but uncertainty clouds the future. “We wanted to take the ship out to the Black Sea before entering the shipyard, but because of that risk, we didn’t enter the Black Sea and didn’t take on any cargo. We’ve been in the shipyard for 50 days for repairs, but we don’t know what will happen once the repairs are finished,” the superintendent said. Turkish shipowners warn that many are on the brink of bankruptcy, as idle ships rack up costs of up to 50,000 euros a month in mooring and crew expenses. Ziya Ustel, CEO of Turkish shipping company VI-ZA STAR, says high freight rates are being offered for Black Sea routes, but the risks are too great. “They are offering high freight rates, etc,” Ustel said. Without a diplomatic solution, few shipowners will be prepared to risk their vessels, Ustel warned. “The main thing is to find out a real solution,” Ustel added. “Otherwise, no one will try anything anymore.” Turkish diplomacy Ankara is expected to step up its efforts to find a solution. Grain brokers say hopes of a diplomatic breakthrough may be one reason prices have so far remained below the record highs seen at the start of the war. But if Turkish efforts fail and attacks on Black Sea shipping continue, higher grain prices could have a considerable impact, especially on the world’s poorest nations, many of which depend on Russian and Ukrainian grain. https://www.dw.com/en/germany-shaken-by-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Nqtu Former BND chief August Hanning has been arrested on espionage charges Image: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement If the allegations are confirmed, it would be an espionage case of historic proportions for Germany: August Hanning, former head of the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) , has been arrested , with the federal prosecutor accusing him of espionage, treason and attempted treason. August Hanning , now 80, headed the BND from 1998 to 2005. But even before then, he had enjoyed a meteoric rise within the security apparatus. After leaving the BND, he served as state secretary in the Federal Interior Ministry, then moved into the private sector and worked as a security consultant. According to the federal prosecutor's office , his informant was his former chief-of-staff, named in the statement only as Manfred D.*, who went on to hold this position under Hanning's successors from March 2012 to March 2026. D. thus had access to a great deal of classified information. DW's Michaela Küfner looks at Germany's espionage scandal To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Classified information from the chancellor's office Manfred D. is alleged to have passed on nearly 2,000 BND documents — some of them highly sensitive — to Hanning over the course of several years in exchange for money. Hanning is then said to have used the information in his private consultancy business. The most serious allegation is that Hanning is said to have maintained close contact with an employee of a foreign intelligence service for years and to have leaked classified information to him. It is not known which country was involved, but reports say it is not Russia. Investigators also mention an analysis that Hanning is said to have prepared for an employee of another foreign intelligence service. However, it is not certain whether the analysis ever reached that person. The classified information also concerned the routine meetings of the heads of German security agencies at the chancellery. Topics included, among other things, the Iranian nuclear program and analyses of the Russian armed forces. Since intelligence from foreign partner agencies is also said to have been shared in this context, this could also undermine their trust in the German BND and lead to difficulties in future intelligence cooperation with Germany. Hanning came under scrutiny in an entirely different context "A good agent is one who doesn't draw attention to himself," Hanning was once quoted as saying. When he finally drew attention to himself, it was in an entirely different context. In September 2025, the Hamburg state police searched Hanning's home and offices in connection with the famous case of the kidnapping involving Christina Block , heiress to the steakhouse restaurant chain Block House. State prosecutors in Hamburg accused her of having ordered the kidnapping of her two youngest children in late 2023 due to a custody dispute. A little over a year before the operation to bring the children back, there is said to have already been a failed kidnapping attempt. At the time, there were suspicions that Hanning was involved, which he denies. But during a search in 2025, investigators found an electronic storage device containing top-secret BND documents. The police handed the documents over to the federal prosecutor's office, which launched a covert investigation against Hanning and Manfred D. in May 2026. The most recent documents found so far are said to date from June 2022. Greens demand consequences Throughout its history, the BND has seen a number of espionage cases, some of them spectacular. In the 1960s, Heinz Felfe headed the "Counterintelligence: Soviet Union" division while simultaneously working for the Soviet secret service, the KGB. In 2014, a BND employee was exposed as a spy for the US CIA. There is also an ongoing trial against a BND agent accused of betraying secrets to Russia's FSB in September and October 2022 — that is, after the start of the war in Ukraine. Yet never before has a former official of August Hanning's stature been at the center of suspicion of espionage. "The BND launched extensive internal investigations early on and without delay, which corroborated the suspicions," said current BND President Martin Jäger. "For the BND and for me, there can be no compromises when it comes to internal security." However, there was some fierce criticism from the political sphere. Günter Krings of the conservative governing party, the Christian Democratic Union (CDU), told the Rheinische Post newspaper: "The mere suspicion that a former BND chief is selling secrets is damaging to trust in our security agencies." Konstantin von Notz of the environmentalist Green Party and deputy chair of the parliamentary committee that oversees the intelligence services said: "These are serious and grave allegations that have been leveled against August Hanning." Speaking on behalf of his party, he called for greater scrutiny of lobbying activities by former top officials and those with the highest security clearances. "These are clearly also a gateway for hostile intelligence services," von Notz said. The federal government must put an immediate stop to these "illegitimate practices." Clara Bünger, domestic policy spokesperson for the socialist Left Party group in the Bundestag , went even further: "The investigations against former BND chief Hanning show once again: The intelligence services themselves are a security risk." This article was originally written in German. *Editor's note: DW follows the German press code, which stresses the importance of protecting the privacy of suspected criminals or victims and urges us to refrain from revealing full names in such cases. Saudi Arabia is dealing with the aftermath of a series of deadly attacks, including two strikes on Riyadh's international airport over the weekend that killed 14 people. A missile attack on King Khalid International Airport on Saturday killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300 , according to Saudi authorities. A second strike on Sunday killed a Pakistani national and injured at least 11 others. Saudi authorities also reported damage from an attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, near Bahrain and Qatar. The Houthis claimed responsibility for the attacks, warning that Saudi airports and airspace were "legitimate targets," except for the Muslim holy cities of Mecca and Medina. The group said it had targeted the two airports, a gas plant and an Aramco oil refinery using missiles and drones. Its claims could not be independently verified. Turkey, Egypt, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia jointly condemned the attacks as a violation of Saudi sovereignty and a threat to civilian safety. The attacks came amid an escalation in fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen. Saudi Arabia has intensified its airstrikes, while the Houthis have warned that further attacks could follow. US President Donald Trump said over the weekend that Washington was considering joining Saudi military operations against the Houthis. Iran, meanwhile, offered to help facilitate talks between Saudi Arabia and Yemen.
